newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Broke but armed, Albania city set to vote.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Broke but armed, Albania city set to vote.

text.p: In his ransacked office, Medin Xhelili ponders how to fit some half a million signatures onto 24 sheets of paper for Albania's June 29 elections.

"Every photocopied page costs 10 leks (6 cents) but the commune doesn't have it," Xhelili, district council chairman for the southern port city of Vlore, said in his office, which was looted of all but a few books and papers during riots in March.

Xhelili had just returned from the capital Tirana where he was given one copy of the 27-page election law to serve Vlore and nearby communes, and 24 sheets of paper on which the names of Vlore's 120,000 voters must be handwritten in quadruplicate.
"I don't know where the money is but our government will have to give it to us," Xhelili said.
"I have heard the U.S. will give $12 million (for the elections)...But the situation in Vlore is very grave."
That is an understatement in this city where the riots that brought down Albania's Democratic Party-led government began.
Some 150 people were killed in Vlore and nearby communes in riots sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes that wiped out many peoples' life savings.

After the riots, the international community led by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) pushed Albania to name a multi-party interim government and hold early elections to stabilise the turbulent Balkan country.

Despite empty municipal coffers and an estimated one million weapons looted from armouries in the hands of citizens, election planning is going ahead "like a train without brakes running downhill", said one adviser to the OSCE, which will monitor the vote.
LAWLESS VLORE

Conditions for holding elections in Vlore, a city of 80,000 to 100,000 people, are anything but ideal. Whole blocks of shops have been looted, some torched. Other stores wedged between the looted shops seem to be permanently shuttered.
In the morning, streets are alive with people coming out to buy food at kiosks and children going to school. But at 4 p.m. everyone rushes home because the streets turn dangerous.

Residents of Vlore, who blamed President Sali Berisha and the then-Democratic Party run government for financial havoc wreaked by the pyramid schemes, ran out the police and smashed windows of the now-deserted police headquarters.

The central government's authority ends at a bridge 20 km (12 miles) north of Vlore. Heavily armed gangs who may have anything from Kalashnikovs to heavy machineguns rule the city from late afternoon into the night, residents say.
One section of the city is said to be run by 27-year-old Sazan Caushi, who goes by the name "Zani" and has cultivated a Robin Hood-style image in the international press.

Xhelili, 49, says Zani's power has been exaggerated, but he does not conceal his frustration that a 6,000-strong Italian-led multinational force, sent to Albania in April to protect aid supplies, has not intervened more forcefully.
"It has never happened before in the history of Albania that the members of the armed forces of eight countries are present here," he said. "We have to ask why have they come?
"We are very dissatisfied as far as the establishment of law and order is concerned. So again, I ask, why have they come?"
"We are not the police," said Lieutenant Colonel Gianfranco Scalas, spokesman for the 1,100-man mostly Italian brigade stationed on the Adriatic beachfront.
Scalas said the force, sent to Albania in April to protect aid supplies, is not there to confiscate weapons, round up criminals or protect candidates.
"The barber shops are open again and when a barber shop opens for business that's a good sign," Scalas said.
"Within Vlore right now our presence during the night and day is very intensive which means we are having an impact on security," he added.
But residents still fume about the collapse of the pyramid schemes and talk does not bode well for peaceful campaigning.
In May 1996 elections, condemned as fraudulent by Europe and the United States, Vlore voted for Berisha. Today he is unwelcome.
"If he comes here it would be cause for war," said Besnik Kendezi, a local Socialist Party leader meeting friends in a cafe.
"Berisha is trying to get at least a third of the vote so that he could defeat a motion of no-confidence and stay in office," he said. "But if he stays he will be the gangrene of Albanian politics."
LOCAL ECONOMY AT STANDSTILL

Seated across the table, Edmond Shenediela said Vlore's economy has come almost to a complete standstill since the pyramid schemes -- which in some cases promised up to 200 percent return on investments -- collapsed.
"The word 'work' doesn't exist, we're entering a deep crisis," he said.
"It used to be the only means of living was the percentage we got from the pyramids. Now there is some construction work but otherwise there is no future, no equipment."

The pyramid schemes, in which Albanians were said to have lost up to $1.5 billion, or more than half the country's annual Gross Domestic Product, gave Vlore hundreds of satellite dishes which sprout from balcony after balcony and rooftop after rooftop. But what the schemes gave they also took away.
Jolanda Andrecka, 46, said her husband's job as a night watchman ended when the man whose house he was guarding lost his property after the pyramid schemes collapsed.
Now the family of five lives on what she can glean as caretaker of Vlore's Orthodox church, which served as a fire station in communist times, and aid from relief agencies.
"Before we had the pyramid companies -- I did not have investments in them, but many did," she said. "Now everybody has gone bankrupt and there is no work."
